title: The River That Remembers
summary: An old woman teaches a ferryman that the Zambezi keeps the names of everyone who has ever asked it for passage.
moral: The river remembers what we ask of it, and what we give back.
attribution: A traditional Tonga tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A baobab beside broad river bands, a small canoe and a low sun

sentences.text: The Zambezi does not widen easily; it gathers its water and then takes it away in a hurry.
The Tonga tell of a ferryman who knew every current from the rapids to the shallows, and who had carried people across for so long that he no longer remembered a life before the canoe.
One evening an old woman came to the bank with a clay pot on her head and asked to cross.
There was a storm coming, and the ferryman told her to wait until morning.
“The river is angry,” he said.
The old woman shook her head.
“The river is not angry,” she said.
“It is remembering.
Let us go.”
They crossed with the water pushing at the canoe from every side.
The ferryman paddled as he had never paddled before, and the old woman spoke quietly to the river, and every name she spoke seemed to calm a stretch of the water just ahead of them.
On the far bank the ferryman asked her whose names she had been saying.
“The names of the people who crossed here before you,” said the old woman.
“Your river keeps them.
It keeps the ones who asked for passage and the ones who gave nothing, and it does not tell them apart unless you do.”
The ferryman thought about this.
After that he kept a gourd on the bank, and everyone who crossed left a little grain, a little milk, or a little salt in it.
When the gourd was full, he carried it to the old woman’s village, and the village fed the ferryman and his family in return.
The river still remembers.
At the place where the ferryman kept his gourd the water is said to be gentler than anywhere else on that bend.
The old people say this is not because the river is kind, but because it has been greeted properly.
